title: Staff Only
subtitle: A volcano resort on press day, after dark
story:
The resort on the volcano island opened to guests this spring. Its owner mines the sulfur that burns blue in the crater, runs night tours on catwalks above the vents, and tells every reporter that his eruption alarm is 99 percent accurate. You came for the press day. Tonight there is a red glow under the blue fire, and most of the staff have quietly left the mountain.

Slip away from the tour and find the owner's monitoring record: the training days he built the alarm on, and this season's held-back days, which he never published. From them, work out the probability that an eruption follows within the week. Predict the held-back days. Find which reading drives the risk. Then count the eruption days the alarm caught and the ones it missed. If the mountain is building, you need to know whether the alarm would say so.

Pick a side by the door you take at the start: one of you takes the control side (the seismic readings), the other the machine side (the gas readings). Neither half proves it alone. Each of you copies your half onto the press-kit USB stick you were given. Then carry it onto the last monorail car of the night, down to the harbor hotel on the coast. Miss that car and you are on the crater until morning.

escapeBrief: Staff Only. Two journalists on the resort's press day slip away from the night tour to prove the villain's volcano is unsafe while guests walk the catwalks over the blue fire. They start in the orange overalls and visitor badges every guest and reporter is issued. Every staff door has a scanner with a needle on an S-shaped dial and its own entry log: rows of little figures in their outfits, each admitted or refused, by day (sun) or night (moon). The logs teach, with no written instructions, that what you wear decides what opens: one item decides (yellow hat; black armband), an item that varies freely means nothing, two items add up (gray overalls plus plant badge), and the rule can differ by day and night (server room: white hat by day, blue by night). The tour guide says outright: our team wear orange. ESCAPE (not split). Night, red glow rising. Both reach the monorail platform carrying the press-kit USB stick, now holding the villain's real monitoring data in place of the safety brochure. The gate admits staff only and shows its own log of fifteen entries. Orange is on everyone, admitted or refused, so it means nothing. By day any staff badge passes; at night only the night maintenance crew rides, and every night admit wears the engineer's badge and the purple armband, in any overalls and any hat. The day look (guide badge) is refused at night, and so is each of the two items alone. The player dresses from the station locker room beside the platform (four slots: overalls, hats, armbands, badges; 600 outfits) and is scanned. The needle moves live; three refused scans trip a lockdown back to the locker room. Engineer badges are only in the station badge locker, released by the control-side player's final puzzle; the gate has no power until the machine-side player's final puzzle. Unguessability: the permutations (20 of 600 outfits pass at night) plus the scan limit. Echo: which predictors drive the call, and the rare case decides it, applied to an unknown: yourselves. Ending: the monorail runs down to the harbor hotel, the story breaks, the guests are taken off the island.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: This scenario was classification with logistic regression: predicting the probability of a yes-or-no outcome from several measured predictors, then scoring those predictions on days held back from the model, where a rare outcome means a model can be right on almost every day and still miss the days that matter. Here is what you did.

escapeHints.text: Every scanner door you passed has a log board beside it, and so does the monorail gate on the platform. The gate's log is the one that matters now.
Read only the night rows of the gate's log. What do the people it let through at night have on that the people it refused do not?
At night the gate weighs just two of the four things you can wear, and it does not care about the rest. Every night admit is wearing both of those two; no night refusal is wearing both.

done.title: The proof is on the stick
done.body: Both halves of his record are on the press-kit stick. His 99 percent came from a calm year, and on this season's eruption days his alarm stayed quiet almost every time. The red glow under the blue fire is still rising. The last monorail car of the night waits at the crater platform, but after dark it carries staff only, and the gate checks what you are wearing.

control.title: Your half of the record
control.body: The seismic half of his record is done. Copy it onto the press-kit stick at the copy station here before you go. Down on the crater rim the station is still dark: your partner's half will light its gate panel with a number for you to key in. Behind the locker-room door the tall steel locker has sprung open, and the tag inside its door carries a number your partner needs.

machine.title: Your half of the record
machine.body: The gas half of his record is done. Copy it onto the press-kit stick at the cable cabinet here before you go. Up on the crater rim the station has power: the gate panel is lit with a number your partner needs, and the locker-room door is open. escapeDone.title: The last car down
escapeDone.body: The gate's needle swings past the line and the doors slide open. The car drops away from the crater, the blue fire and the red glow shrinking behind you and the lights of the harbor hotel growing below. By morning the story is out, and boats are taking the guests off the island.

rooms.debrief: This puzzle asked whether being right on most days makes a warning system useful. Eruptions follow only a small share of days, so an alarm that almost never sounds is right almost every day. Counting only the days that were followed by an eruption, and asking which of them each system called, measures what a warning is for.

rooms.designNote: BOSS (MACHINE), red 3. catwalk control room PUZZLE SPEC, transcribed from _scratch/ladder_spec_draft.md -> MACHINE BOSS. Shared setup (the chapter teaches filter() on record): training_days <- crater_monitoring %>% filter(record == "training"); held_back_days <- crater_monitoring %>% filter(record == "held back"). predictWithModel() adds probability_yes and predicted_class (cut-off 0.5). ANSWER, TOLERANCE/MARGIN AND THE TEMPTING READINGS: _scratch/ladder_spec_draft.md and _scratch/ladder_key.csv ONLY (scenario.json is published; never copy them here). PROMPT: Most days are not followed by an eruption, so a system that always says "no" is right most of the time. Score your gas model at the 0.5 cut-off and "always no" on the held-back days. Which is right on more days? Now count what matters: of the held-back days followed by an eruption within the week, on how many did your model say yes? Store that number of days in `answer`. CODE: gas_predictions %>% summarize(model_right = sum(predicted_class == eruption_within_week), always_no_right = sum(eruption_within_week == "no")); gas_predictions %>% filter(eruption_within_week == "yes", predicted_class == "yes") %>% count(). Its west door opens onto the spine's W run out to the acid lake jetty (m_lake): a real depicted door, open both ways, never gated on the boss.

ladderPlain.text: In the first control-side puzzle you fit a logistic regression on the training days with tremor level as its one predictor, and read the probability it gave one named day of being followed by an eruption within the week.

In the second you fit all four seismic predictors on the training days, used the model to predict the held-back days it had never seen, and picked out the day it rated most likely, with the 0.5 cut-off marked on your plot.

In the third you scaled the four seismic predictors before fitting, so their coefficients could be compared fairly, and picked the one that moves the probability most, which is not the one with the largest coefficient before scaling.

In the final control-side puzzle you scored your model and the resort's alarm on the held-back days, found the alarm right on more of them, and then counted the eruption days your model called and the alarm missed, the count that shows which of the two actually warns.
In the first machine-side puzzle you fit a logistic regression on the training days with sulfur dioxide output as its one predictor, and read the probability it gave one named day.
In the second you fit all five gas and heat predictors on the training days, used the model to predict the held-back days, and picked out the day it rated most likely.
In the third you scaled the five predictors before fitting and picked the one that moves the probability most, which is not the one with the largest coefficient before scaling.

In the final machine-side puzzle you set your model against a rule that always says no, found the rule right on more of the held-back days while calling none of the eruptions, and counted the eruption days your model did call.

To get out you read the monorail gate's log of who it let through by day and by night, worked out which two of the four things you can wear it weighs at night, and wore those two through the gate with the record on the stick.
